> Estimate the Level-2 variance of Reaction (its Level-2 component is the random intercepts)
>
> model2 <- '
>     level: 1
>         Reaction ~ Days
>         Reaction ~~ var.L1*Reaction
>    level: 2
>         Reaction ~~ var.L2*Reaction
> '

Thanks Terrence - that’s what I was looking for!

> Note that by only include Days in the Level-1 model, you are estimating the conflated effect of Days, in both the MLM and MLSEM.  In lmer(), decomposing the effects would require calculating cluster means for Days, then cluster-mean-centering Days (manifest covariate approach).  But MLSEM can use the latent covariate approach, automatically decomposing Level-1 predictors into their level-specific components.  Then you can define the contextual effect and test whether the effect differs across levels.  Also, the R-squared at each level will then correspond to the pseudo-R-squared per level calculated from residual-variance reduction in MLM (although the Level-2 R-squared will be attenuated in MLM due to unreliability of cluster-mean estimates; Lüdtke et al., 2008 <https://doi.org/10.1037/a0012869>,  2011 <https://doi.org/10.1037/a0012869>).
>

> model2 <- '
>     level: 1
>         Reaction ~ b1*Days
>         Reaction ~~ var.L1*Reaction
>    level: 2
>         Reaction ~ b2*Days
>         Reaction ~~ var.L2*Reaction
>

>   contextual := b2 - b1 # contextual effect

> ‚

This gives me the following error:

Error in S[1, 1] : incorrect number of dimensions

Any ideas?

-Felix

messages.body_plain:
Thanks so much for your feedback. So your advice is that if I keep with the wlsmv estimator I should use the Wu and Estabrook procedure and use   measEq.syntax ?

Otherwise, if I decide to use the MLR estimator, can I follow the script below using lavaan?

# model 1: configural invariance age_group

fit1 <- cfa(PCL.model1001, data = pcl_ti_data_amostra1001,  estimator = "MLR",  group = "age_group")

# model 2: metric (weak) invariance age_group

fit2 <- cfa(PCL.model1001, data=pcl_ti_data_amostra1001, estimator="MLR",  group="age_group",group.equal="loadings")

# model 3: scalar (strong) invariance age_group

fit3 <- cfa(PCL.model1001, data=pcl_ti_data_amostra1001, estimator="MLR",  group="age_group", group.equal=c("loadings", "thresholds"))

Mirtes Garcia Pereira
Coordenadora do Programa de Pós-graduação
em Ciências Biomédicas (Fisiologia e Farmacologia)
Laboratório de Neurofisiologia do Comportamento
Departamento de Fisiologia e Farmacologia
Universidade Federal Fluminense

Em qui., 31 de mar. de 2022 às 18:06, Terrence Jorgensen <tjorge...@gmail.com> escreveu:

> > configural, metric and scalar invariance using WLSMV estimator
>
> If you rely on the latent-response assumption of the threshold model, loadings are not comparable (not on the same metric) until AFTER you constrain thresholds to equality.  See references on the ?semTools::measEq.syntax help page, and see Examples there.
>
>
> > if I change the estimator to MLR and ordered=FALSE, to test scalar invariance  should I change  group.equal=c("loadings", "thresholds"))  to group.equal=c("loadings", "intercepts")) as data  will be considered as continuous?
>
> Yes, but even with WLSMV (threshold model for categorical indicators), you can test equivalence of loadings then intercepts, AFTER first testing equivalence of thresholds.  I am aware there is plenty of faulty literature out there that perpetuates the misconception that thresholds are the ordinal equivalent of intercepts, but that is misinformation.
>
> Terrence D. Jorgensen
> Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
> Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.body_plain:
> Error in S[1, 1] : incorrect number of dimensions
>
> Any ideas?

Not sure what causes it, but when you set fixed.x=FALSE to treat Days as random (not really the case), you will get results.  However, the Level-2 parameters don't have SEs and the estimates are wacky, so I don't think it converges on an actual solution.  At first, I thought the problem might be the low Level-2 N=18, but the real problem is that because everyone had exactly the same Days values, there is no Level-2 variance of the Days "cluster" means:

aggregate(Days ~ Subject, data = sleepstudy, mean) # all are 4.5 (Days == 1:9)

So in this particular example, there is no opportunity for the Level-1 predictor to explain Level-2 variance, which confuses the optimizer when we try.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.subject_clean: structural part ruins the measurement part
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am running multigroup cfa with binary indicators and intercepts, loadings, thresholds, and residuals invariance. Everything works OK. (Here I don’t try to test invariance, just postulate it).

But when I add a structural part model to my measurement model, the warnings about correlation between indicators appear. The problem arises with almost every set of variables in the structural part.

My full model contains more groups and three additional factors (with numeric indicators) and there are warnings about correlation between almost every possible pair of indicators (binary and binary, or binary and numeric).

I wonder how is it possible that the structural part ruins the measurement part, and what should I do in this case?

Thank you both for your helpful explanation and comments! Apologize for the delayed responses.

Two questions I now have are:
1. Can I test structural invariance (i.e., latent variance and covariance) on the basis of scalar invariance? Or do I have to achieve strict invariance before moving forward with structural invariance testing. My understanding so far is that I can test latent variance and covariance after achieving even metric invariance, but getting some clarification and confirmation would be much appreciated!

2. In my metric, scalar and strict invariance models, I found that many of the residual variances have no standard errors, and some of them have "NA" standard errors. I wonder if this should be a cause of concern? In the configural model, residual variances were estimated and look fine.

On Tuesday, March 29, 2022 at 8:04:50 AM UTC-5 michael....@uniroma1.it wrote:
> Hi,
> my collaborators and I had the same problem when we tried to run a multigroup CFA with an ordinal variable with 3 response cateogories (levels).
> I sent an email to Ryne Estabrook, since he wrote a very nice article on how to conduct multigroup CFA (Wu, H., & Estabrook, R. (2016). Identification of confirmatory factor analysis models of different levels of invariance for ordered categorical outcomes. Psychometrika, 81(4), 1014-1045).
> This is what he texted me back:
>
> "The fact that you’re at three categories (and thus, two thresholds) suggests something to me. Each ordinal item requires two constraints to scale the underlying continuous variable we assume is beneath it. When you constrain your model to have equal thresholds across groups, you’re simply rescaling each variable, which won’t result in any loss of fit. Put differently, there’s no difference in constraining the thresholds for item 1 group 2 to be zero and one or constraining them to be the same as item 1 group 1.
> This issue is the broad point of that paper. There’s no such thing as an unconstrained categorical factor model. You make some constraints to make the model identifiable. Sometimes those constraints interact with other constraints in weird ways. You started at something equivalent to the configurally invariant model, so making that “constraint” didn’t change anything".
>
> Indeed, when I tried another CFA with more than 3 response categories I didn't have this issue anymore.
>
>
> Hope this helps.
>
> Best regards,
>
> Michael Schepisi
>
>
>
> Il giorno lunedì 28 marzo 2022 alle 23:24:43 UTC+2 edward...@gmail.com ha scritto:
> > Strict invariance should include more restrictions, so degrees of freedom should be higher. If chi-square does not increase, this indicates that the test was not able to detect discrepancy between the incremental constraints and the data. That failure may be due to a lack of power or due to the additional constraints actually matching the population covariance matrix. The usual statistical test is a chi-square difference test. But if chi-squares are identical--quite surprising, actually--then the chi-square difference is 0, supporting the additional constraints. CFI incorporates the quantity max ( chi-square - degrees of freedom, 0), so if chi-square does not change but degrees of freedom get larger, this quantity will get smaller, as long as chi-square is greater than degrees of freedom.
> >
> > On Mon, Mar 28, 2022 at 12:36 PM 'Quanfa He' via lavaan <lav...@googlegroups.com> wrote:
> > > Hi,
> > >

> > >

messages.subject: AW: Extract model-implied latent means/variances to calculate Welch t-test for multiple groups
messages.subject_clean: AW: Extract model-implied latent means/variances to calculate Welch t-test for multiple groups
messages.body_plain:
Hi Victoria,

You don't need to extract anything. It is already there. Here is an example for latent means with 2 groups (it should also work with more than 2 groups):

library(lavaan)

HS.model <- '
visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9
'

fit <- cfa(
  model         = HS.model,
  data          = HolzingerSwineford1939,
  meanstructure = TRUE,
  group         = "school",
  group.equal   = c("regressions", "intercepts")
)

pe  <- parameterEstimates(fit)                 # Get parameter estimates
lv  <- lavNames(fit, type = "lv")              # Get latent variables
res <- pe[pe$op == "~1" & pe$lhs %in% lv,]     # Means of latent variables
res                                            # Output

If you only need a simple vector, you can proceed as follows:

coef        <- res$est
names(coef) <- paste(res$lhs, res$op, ".", res$group, sep = "")
coef

Why not use a resampling method like bootstrapping? If you need CI compliant p-values, maybe x.boot could be helpful.

Best

Christian

Von: lav...@googlegroups.com <lav...@googlegroups.com> im Auftrag von Victoria McRitchie <victoria....@gmail.com>
Gesendet: Montag, 4. April 2022 18:03
An: lavaan <lav...@googlegroups.com>
Betreff: Extract model-implied latent means/variances to calculate Welch t-test for multiple groups

Hi everyone,

I have 7 groups and 5 factors in my CFA, and having established partial scalar invariance, I would like to compare the latent means using a Welch's t-test (with Satterthwaite correction for unequal variances).  There will be 105 tests in all (5 factors x 7*6/2 group comparisons). FYI - have constrained all means to be equal but there is no evidence of invariance, so hence why I want to compare the means individually.

So I need to extract from my lavaan model:
a) the 5 latent (unstandardized) means x 7 groups (although one group is constrained to zero as the reference group)
b) the 5 latent (unstandardized) variances x 7 groups

My workaround thus far has been to copy parameters from the summary function and dumping into Excel, but this feels a little clumsy.

How can I get a) and b) above out of the model and into a data frame so that I can then apply my Welch t-test function (which I will create a homemade function for).

Thanks
Victoria

messages.subject: Re: structural part ruins the measurement part
messages.subject_clean: structural part ruins the measurement part
messages.body_plain:
Once you add exogenous covariates, lavaan switches to conditional.x =
TRUE mode. This implies that instead of computing regular
poly/tetra-choric correlations, lavaan computes *residual*
poly/tetra-choric correlations, after regressing out the covariates.

In  your case, it would seem this leads to the following problem:

>            lavaan WARNING: correlation between variables item2 and item1
>         is (nearly) 1.0

So after controlling for the covariates, item1 and item are nearly
identical.

The only way out here is to either remove one of the two items, or
remove the covariate that is causing this.

Yves.

messages.body_plain:
The problem is probably related to missing data:

library(lavaan)
library(nonnest2)

# Simulate data
m.pop <- "Y ~ 1 * x1 + 0.9 * x2 + 0.9 * x3 + 0.8 * x4 + 0.9 * x5 + 0.8 * x6 + 0.9 * x7"

set.seed(1)
df <- simulateData(m.pop, sample.nobs = 1000)

m1 <- "Y ~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4 + x5 + x6"
m2 <- "Y ~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4 + x5 + x6 + x7"

fit1 <- sem(m1, df)
fit2 <- sem(m2, df)

# Run Vuong test ---- works fine

messages.subject: Re: Ridge Option for non-positive definite sample covariance matrix
messages.subject_clean: Ridge Option for non-positive definite sample covariance matrix
messages.body_plain:
Hello Julia,

> 1) What is the difference between the parameters "ridge" and "ridge.x"?
> How to use them?

The documentation AND code for 'ridge' needs updating/fixing indeed. But
the ridge.x option is not used, and should have been removed.

Ridging (if requested) is currently only done for exogenous variables.
The goal was (only) to allow for rank-deficient design matrices. It was
never designed for ridge SEM (as in Yuan & Bentler, 2011).

However, as I just found out, it does not work if you provide the sample
covariance matrix directly! This is a bug that will be fixed soon.

> 2) What does the parameter "sample.icov" do?

If set to FALSE, it avoids the computation of the inverse of the sample
covariance matrix. This is only used internally (in sam()) to handle
special cases where the number of variables is smaller than the number
of observations. It is not supposed to be a user-visible option.

Yves.

messages.subject: Technical question about se = "bootstrap" and bootstrapLavaan
messages.subject_clean: Technical question about se = "bootstrap" and bootstrapLavaan
messages.body_plain:
I have a rather technical question about the bootstrap procedure. I would like to first fit a lavaan model, then bootstrap the model with bootstrapLavaan and pass the results to the fitted lavaan object. I know this serves no immediate practical purpose, it is currently just for my understanding.

Here's what I did:

model <- '
  # measurement model
    ind60 =~ x1 + x2 + x3
    dem60 =~ y1 + y2 + y3 + y4
    dem65 =~ y5 + y6 + y7 + y8
  # regressions
    dem60 ~ ind60
    dem65 ~ ind60 + dem60
  # residual correlations
    y1 ~~ y5
    y2 ~~ y4 + y6
    y3 ~~ y7
    y4 ~~ y8
    y6 ~~ y8
'
fit            <- sem(model, data = PoliticalDemocracy)
set.seed(1)
boot           <- bootstrapLavaan(fit, R = 100)
fit@boot       <- list(coef = boot)
fit@Options$se <- "bootstrap"
parameterEstimates(fit, boot.ci.type = "perc")

This seems to work fine, at least when I compare the SE and CI to the usual approach:

set.seed(1)
fit.boot <- sem(model, data = PoliticalDemocracy, se = "bootstrap", bootstrap = 100)
parameterEstimates(fit.boot, boot.ci.type = "perc")

My question is as follows: Is it sufficient to modify object@boot and object@Options$se in every case, or do other things need to be considered for more complex models?

Best

Christian

The same question holds for age as I originally divided the sample in 5 sub-groups .

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Non positive-definite covariance matrix means that at least one of the variables is an exact linear combination of other variables. In the regression context, this would be a violation of the “no perfect collinearity” assumption. You need to check your data. This will happen in small samples if your sample size is smaller than the number of variables and it can happen by change if you get close to this threshold.

https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/30465/what-does-a-non-positive-definite-covariance-matrix-tell-me-about-my-data

Mikko

I am interested in running a multiple regression model to test the association between a predictor variable x and an outcome variable y and some confounders variables (e. g. gender, age).
Considering that  metric invariance (loadings constrained to be equal across groups) across confounder variables groups (gender, age) is supported for the predictor variable and for the outcome variable, is it ok to run  multiple regression models (examples : binomial negative , logistic regression) or is it necessary to have scalar invariance ( loadings and intercepts constrained) ?
Mirtes Garcia Pereira
Coordenadora do Programa de Pós-graduação
em Ciências Biomédicas (Fisiologia e Farmacologia)
Laboratório de Neurofisiologia do Comportamento
Departamento de Fisiologia e Farmacologia
Universidade Federal Fluminense

messages.subject: Measurement invariance of intensive longitudinal data
messages.subject_clean: Measurement invariance of intensive longitudinal data
messages.body_plain:
Hi all

I have a dataset where each participant has completed a 6 item measure for 7 days at each of three different time points. Ie:

Week x: Day 1 - 7

Week y: Day 1 - 7

Week z: Day 1 - 7

The measurement model of the items is a unidimensional structure. Could someone point me towards an example of how to assess measurement invariance between the three timepoints (i.e. Week x,y and z). The reason that the level "week" is important is because we want to see whether, when participants have a break from the questionnaire between weeks, if this impacts the assumed invariance.

I was looking at multilevel SEM (https://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/multilevel.html) but here I think I have an additional level of clustering (i.e. days nested within weeks nested within participants). I am not sure that this can be handled in Lavaan, and I may need to go to Mplus if not.

Thanks in advance for the help,

Pip

messages.subject: Re: measurement invariance - releasing constraints based on lavTestScore
messages.subject_clean: measurement invariance - releasing constraints based on lavTestScore
messages.body_plain:
> 1- Is this an acceptable way of identifying which constraints should be released?
> 2- The constraints to be released were identified correctly  after checking for their labels in partable?

Seems right to me.  But if scalar invariance still fails, then you have to recursively apply this method.  That's where the trouble starts because score tests are biased when the alternative model is still not correct (i.e., when there is more than 1 item with DIF, the tests for DIF-free items will have inflated Type I error rates).

Something else you could do is check how much the latent-mean estimate changes in group 2 between full- and partial-invariance models.  That quantifies the impact of the DIF on your estimate of interest (see Oberski et al., 2014 <https://doi.org/10.1093/pan/mpv020> for discussion).

> 3- Is the partial scalar variance model correct?

No one can know, but your syntax follows logically from the output, as far as I can tell.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.subject: Re: Multi-level SEM: Zero variance in Clusters/errors
messages.subject_clean: Multi-level SEM: Zero variance in Clusters/errors
messages.body_plain:
> lavaan WARNING: Level-1 variable “item” has no variance within some clusters. The cluster ids with zero within variance are: ID1, ID2.

This can happen, especially frequently with small clusters (not much opportunity for variability, especially with, e.g., 5-point response scales).  If your model converges, you can probably ignore this warning.  It is just letting you know, in case you accidentally put a Level-2 variable in the Level-1 model (in which case, it would have 0 variance within ALL clusters).

> We have zero/negative variance in 60 clusters

How can you have negative variance?  That happens sometimes when estimating residual variances, but your observed variances (sample stats) cannot be negative.

Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

> > never designed for ridge SEM (as in Yuan & Bentler, 2011).
> >
> > However, as I just found out, it does not work if you provide the sample
> > covariance matrix directly! This is a bug that will be fixed soon.
> >
> >> 2) What does the parameter "sample.icov" do?
> >
> > If set to FALSE, it avoids the computation of the inverse of the sample
> > covariance matrix. This is only used internally (in sam()) to handle
> > special cases where the number of variables is smaller than the number
> > of observations. It is not supposed to be a user-visible option.
> >
> > Yves.

messages.subject: Re: invariance measurement with many groups
messages.subject_clean: invariance measurement with many groups
messages.body_plain:
I would not worry too much about the different sample sizes. You can
still test for measurement invariance. Note that if the main interest is
in regression coefficients, you only need weak invariance (ie equal
factor loadings). There is no need to test for strong invariance (ie
equal intercepts+loadings).

Yves.

messages.subject: Re: Which test statistic to use with WLSMV estimation?
messages.subject_clean: Which test statistic to use with WLSMV estimation?
messages.body_plain:
> according to the lavaan Options documentation....
> "the estimators "WLSM" and "WLSMV" imply the "DWLS" estimator (not the "WLS" estimator) with robust standard errors and a mean or mean and variance adjusted test statistic."
> However, the previous paragraph states that there are two possible mean- and variance-adjusted test statistics available, one being the Satterthwaite style "mean.var.adjusted" and one being "scaled.shifted". Does anyone have advice on which to select?

The default is "scaled.shifted", I believe because it is more efficient than the Satterthwaite approach.

http://www.statmodel.com/download/webnotes/webnote10.pdf

> test = "robust"

That is not an option (does not appear in documentation).  Both "mean.var.adjusted" and "scaled.shifted" are robust options available with DWLS estimation.

messages.subject: Re: multilevel moderated mediation(2-1-1 with a level 1 moderator in the second stage)
messages.subject_clean: multilevel moderated mediation(2-1-1 with a level 1 moderator in the second stage)
messages.body_plain:
> I'm trying to do a 2-1-1 moderated mediation analysis

This is problematic in lavaan because there is no way to calculate product terms between the latent within-level or between-level components.  You can do the decomposition yourself (manifest approach): calculate cluster means (between component), then calculate cluster-mean-centered data (within component), and calculate the product terms to model moderating effects.  In your model syntax, only include the respective components in their appropriate level-specific models.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

When the model was:

F1 <-> F2

  number of items to replace is not a multiple of replacement length

Even though there is no beta matrix.

When I constructed the equivalent model:

A <-> B (explicit)
A -> F1, F2
B -> F1, F2
F1 <-> F2 (implicit)

It ran fine.

Yves, if this isn't enough to reproduce it, I can do a full reprex for you.

Hope this helps, and thanks.
Pat

messages.subject: Re: se = "bootstrap" and missing = "fiml"?
messages.subject_clean: se = "bootstrap" and missing = "fiml"?
messages.body_plain:
I think I can answer this question myself (please correct me if I am wrong). While working on something else, I check the code and I believe lavaan just fits the model again in each bootstrap sample using whatever options set in the original call. Therefore, if missing = "fiml" in the call to lavaan/sem/cfa, then missing = "fiml" should be used again in each bootstrap sample.

This is indeed a good thing. As far as I recall, AMOS cannot combine nonparametric bootstrapping with FIML (It has the option to do parametric bootstrapping when missing data is present but this requires more assumptions than nonparametric bootstrapping does.) It's good to know that lavaan can combine both techniques.

-- Shu Fai

messages.subject_clean: NA/NaN Hessian evaluation with endogenous binary variable
messages.body_plain:
Dear Experts,

I am running a pretty large SEM model using lavaan 0.6.11 and I am encountering the following problem.

Most of my variables are questionnaire items that take values 1-5. I use these items to derive some continuous latent variables using the =~ operator. In my model I also have 2 endogenous binary variables that are predicted by these continuous latent variables and some exogenous variables using the ~ operator.

So far, I have been running this model with the following command:

mod_fit <- sem(mod, data = bl, estimator='WLSMV', missing='pairwise', orthogonal = TRUE)

If I do this, the model fits the data well and I have no problems.

However, I would like the fitting to treat my two endogenous binary variables as categorical. If I make the two binary variables categorical with the ordered() command as described in your instructions and then I run the model as above, I get the following error:

mod_fit <- sem(mod, data = bl, estimator='WLSMV', missing='pairwise', orthogonal = TRUE)

Error in nlminb(start = cache$theta, objective = minObjective, gradient = minGradient,  :
  NA/NaN Hessian evaluation
In addition: Warning messages:
1: In lav_data_full(data = data, group = group, cluster = cluster,  :
  lavaan WARNING: 14 cases were deleted due to missing values in
          exogenous variable(s), while fixed.x = TRUE.
2: In lav_data_full(data = data, group = group, cluster = cluster,  :
  lavaan WARNING: some cases are empty and will be ignored:
  61 79 101 115 130 185 192 197
3: In sqrt(evar) : NaNs produced
4: In sqrt(evar) : NaNs produced

Would you have any insights into what I might be doing wrong?

I have noticed that removing "missing='pairwise'" makes the model run, so can one only get listwise deletion when using endogenous categorical variables?

Thank you very much,

Leonardo Tozzi

messages.subject_clean: lavaan WARNING: some estimated ov variances are negative
messages.body_plain:
Hi Yashi

I took a look at your model and tried fitting it with simulated data. I obtain the same error and a bad fit as well with a sample of 42 observations.

Regarding the bad fit. If I choose to simulate a larger data set (e.g., 100), then the fit measures become better.

Regarding the error. I tried using bounded estimation and it resolved the error (though it is typically used in cases of nonconvergence). You might want to have a look at the paper and use it. Paper: https://doi.org/10.1080/10705511.2021.1982716

Have a look at the code I provided below. One warning about the simulated data: it may be different and 'easier' to  fit then your own data.

I hope this helps finding out the problem.

Best wishes,

Jasper Bogaert
PhD student and teaching assistant
Department of Data Analysis (PP01)
Faculty of Psychology and Educational Sciences
Ghent University
​

---------------------------

code:

### load packages
library(lavaan)
library(semPlot)

### specify model
model <- '

Attitude =~ ATB1 + ATB2 + ATB3
PBC =~ PBC1+ PBC2 + PBC3 + PBC4 + PBC5 + PBC6
SubNorms=~ SN1 + SN2 + SN3 + SN4 + SN5
EConcern =~ EC1 + EC2 + EC3
EVOIntent =~ RPI1 + RPI2 + RPI3

PBC ~ 1*EVOIntent
Attitude ~ 1.5*EVOIntent
SubNorms ~   0.3*EVOIntent
EConcern  ~ 1*EVOIntent
'

n <- 42 # choose sample size
dat <- simulateData(model, sample.nobs = n) # you might need to resimulate the data untill you get the error

### fit model without bounds
fit <- sem(model, data = dat)
summary(fit, fit.measures = T, standardized = T)
lavInspect(fit, "cov.lv <http://cov.lv>")

semPaths(fit)

### fit model with bounds
fit.bounds <- sem(model, data = dat, bounds = "standard")
summary(fit.bounds, fit.measures = T, standardized = T)
lavInspect(fit.bounds, "cov.lv <http://cov.lv>")

messages.subject_clean: Multiple mediation model with a dichotomous predictor
messages.body_plain:
Hello guys,

I'm trying to specify the following model in lavaan:

Where condition is binary (either control or experimental group); and where both the mediators (habits, attitudes, system) and the outcome variable (intention) are all measured on a scale ranging from 1 to 7 ("not at all - very")*.

(*a quick aside here: can the scale be treated is continuous instead of ordinal? Would I want that? If so, why? If not, why not?)

Basically, what I'm trying to see is whether the link between condition and intention remains significant after controlling for the mediators.

(I used the approach they used here <https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0022103118300465>. I attach their supplementary material. On page 12 and 13 is their mediation model.)

I could produce the above plot using lavaanPlot with the following model specifications, which I modelled after this tutorial <https://paolotoffanin.wordpress.com/2017/05/06/multiple-mediator-analysis-with-lavaan/>:

multimedmed <- '#direct effect
intention~b1*habits+b2*attitudes+b3*system+c*condition
#mediators
habits~a1*condition
attitudes~a2*condition
system~a3*condition
indirect1:= a1*b1
indirect2:= a2*b2
indirect3:= a3*b3
#total effect
total:=c+(a1*b1)+(a2*b2)+(a3*b3)
habits~~attitudes
habits~~system
system~~attitudes'

However, to let the model run, I simply changed the condition from a factor to numeric (which is not interpretable, I think) to avoid the "unordered factor(s) with more than two levels detected as exogenous covariate(s): condition" error, as I wanted to simply specify the model for a preregistration of a student project, without actually having the data yet (I just needed the graphic).

Having the data now, I noticed on lavaan website <https://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/cat.html> that one must specify the exogenous categorical variables as dummy variables, which I could do for my dataset using psych's package dummy.code function.

Where I'm lost (due to not really understanding the machinery) is how to adapt the above model, which has the groups collapsed into one variable, into one where the two groups are used instead.

Any help with specifying the model is appreciated (as well as any other resources that could help me do so - I really don't understand the syntax for the mediation model in lavaan).

test_version <- function(version) {

  renv::use(paste0("lavaan@", version))

  estimates <- lavaan_fit |> parameterestimates()
  select_est <- estimates[

      estimates$rhs == "sp7" &
      estimates$op != "~*~",
  ]
  param_est <- select_est$est

    version = version,
    iterations = lavaan_fit |> lavInspect("iterations"),
    converged = lavaan_fit |> lavInspect("converged")
  ) |>
    append(fitmeasures(lavaan_fit, c("chisq", "chisq.scaled"))) |>
    append(param_est) |>
    as.data.frame()
}

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

Could you please help me figure out what the meaning of the ~~ operator is on lavaan in the example below?

Model <- '
# regression 1
Y ~ X + W
# regression 2
X ~ Z + W

Y~~NA*X
`

Does Y~~NA*X allow to compute the correlation between the error terms (i.e., the residuals from the OLS regressions 1 and 2)?
Alternatively, does Y~~NA*X compute the correlation between the two raw variables Y and X?

Many thanks
Ale Dea

Hi Mauricio,

Thank you very much for your posts. As a psych student, I learned a lot from this thread when conducting my own analysis. Though, I still have some questions, could you possibly help?

I wondered:
Why should I include std.lv <http://std.lv> = T? I thought the right way is to fix the first loading to 1.0 and freely estimate others?
I excluded estimator = “MLR” because it gave me a warning, but why? When should I use it? (I read the function description and still didn’t understand)
For a brief background, I'm estimating the level and slope of well-being across 3 waves of data, where well-being was measured by a group of same 5 manifest variables at each wave. I encountered the same lv variances are negative error as Manuel, but adding std.lv <http://std.lv> = T solved it.

I'd greatly appreciate it if you could help clarify!
Tingshu

> > > > > >
> > > > > > # * 3.1 Steinmetz, 2014 ---------------------------------------------------
> > > > > >
> > > > > > # corrected chi-square differences test
> > > > > > CorrDiff <- function(fit.baseline, fit.restricted) # basline = model with less degrees of freedom
> > > > > > {
> > > > > >   Corrc2Base <- fitMeasures(fit.baseline)[[6]] # corrected chi-square value
> > > > > >   MLc2Base <- fitMeasures(fit.baseline)[[3]] # uncorrected chi-square value
> > > > > >   dfBase <- fitMeasures(fit.baseline)[[4]] # degrees of freedom
> > > > > >
> > > > > >   Corrc2Rest <- fitMeasures(fit.restricted)[[6]]
> > > > > >   MLc2Rest <- fitMeasures(fit.restricted)[[3]]
> > > > > >   dfRest <- fitMeasures(fit.restricted)[[4]]
> > > > > >
> > > > > >   c0 <- MLc2Rest / Corrc2Rest
> > > > > >   c1 <- MLc2Base / Corrc2Base
> > > > > >   cd <- (dfRest*c0-dfBase*c1)/(dfRest-dfBase)
> > > > > >   CorrDiff <- (MLc2Rest-MLc2Base)/cd # corrected difference test statistic T_d^*
> > > > > >   dfDiff <- dfRest - dfBase
> > > > > >   pDiff <- 1-pchisq(CorrDiff, dfDiff)
> > > > > >   result <- list(Corr.chisq.difference = CorrDiff,
> > > > > >                  df.difference=dfDiff, p.value=pDiff)
> > > > > >   return(result)
> > > > > > }
> > > > > >
> > > > > > # model comparison
> > > > > > CorrDiff(fit_configural_boredom, fit_weak_boredom)
> > > > > > CorrDiff(fit_weak_boredom, fit_strong_boredom)

messages.subject: Too Many Modification Indices Included in Multilevel-SEM in lavaan?
messages.subject_clean: Too Many Modification Indices Included in Multilevel-SEM in lavaan?
messages.body_plain:
Hi lavaan group,

I have a question about specifying additional item-level residual covariances as suggested by modification indices while conducting MSEM in lavaan.

1. I ran an initial confirmatory measurement model which demonstrated poor fit with the data. [CFI=.747; RMSEA=.042, p<.05, SRMR: within=.073, between=.106].

2. Then, I ran successive models by including a few residual covariances each time based on the previous model’s modification indices (from a subset of modification indices where the mi value was greater than 5).

To protect the interpretation of the model, I only added residual covariances for items measuring the same construct (e.g., between calm and excited or excited and enthusiastic for positive affect), and did not add any residual covariances at the item level across different measures (e.g. between calm and dull or excited and anxious, measuring positive and negative affect respectively). Any other theoretically meaningless modification indices were not included.

3. If I am remembering correctly, Daniel Bauer and Patrick Curran have mentioned the whack-a-mole problem in their SEM workshops suggesting that adding problematic residual covariances based on modification indices regarding one part of the model can sometimes lead to misspecification in other parts of the model.

Attempted solution: To buffer against this problem, I improved my measurement model through several iterations with a small batch of theoretically meaningful modification indices in each successive model; 6 batches of residual covariances at level 1 and 7 batches at level 2, added one batch at a time in several successive models. Batch 1 consisted of a subset of conceptually meaningful modification indices with an mi>100, batch 2 was mi 50-100, batch 3 was 25-50, and the remaining batches were mi 5-25.

At level 1, a total of 29 items (indicators) were included (representing 4 latent constructs). At level 2, a total of 65 items were included (representing 8 latent constructs). For all models, full information maximum likelihood was used and std.lv <http://std.lv> was set to TRUE.

In total, the number of item-level (i.e., indicator-level) residual covariances added across both levels 1 (within-person) and 2 (between-person) were 117. The breakdown of how many residual covariances were added in the model-building procedure at each step is as follows:

Batch: # of residual covariances added
[fit indices where they are retrievable]
The initial confirmatory measurement model
[CFI=.747; RMSEA=.042, p<.05, SRMR: within=.073, between=.106]
Batch 1: Level-1=11; Level-2=5 (mi>100)
Batch 2: Level-1=4; Level-2=5 (100>mi>50)
Batch 3: Level-1=2; Level-2=4 (50>mi>25)
[CFI=.915; RMSEA=.026, p<.05, SRMR: within=.046, between=.095]
Batch 4: Level-1=5; Level-2=10 (mi>5)
Batch 5: Level-1=16; Level-2=21 (mi>5) [SEM with regression equations]
[CFI=.911; RMSEA=.025, p<.05, SRMR: within=.044, between=.090]
Batch 6: Level-1=1; Level-2=9 (mi>5) [SEM with regression equations]
[CFI=.918; RMSEA=.024, p<.05, SRMR: within=.044, between=.088]
Batch 7: Level-1=0; Level-2=24 (mi>5) [SEM with regression equations]
[CFI=.921; RMSEA=.023, p<.05, SRMR: within=.046, between=.083]
Same model but a CFA (and not SEM) without regression equations: [CFI=.938; RMSEA=.022, p<.05; SRMR: within=.044, between=.084]
Total number of residual covariances added: 117 [Level-1=39; Level-2=78]

4. Through this approach overall, I reported findings from an SEM where the model showed good fit [batch 7 model above; CFI=.921; RMSEA=.023, p<.05, SRMR: within=.046, between=.083]. Adding any successive meaningful modification indices was not helping improve model fit much.

5. Kline (2015) also noted in his book that adding too many residual covariances can lead to over-parametrization/over-fitting of the model which can generate results that are not replicable by others.
Attempted solution: To account for this possibility, I ran two MSEM models with regression equations at both levels 1 and 2. The first MSEM model was simply the initial measurement model that showed poor fit (CFI=.747) with the addition of regression equations. The second MSEM model was based on the final model that showed good fit with the data (CFI=.921). The findings of the study overall did not differ between the two models. Some of the regression coefficients were different at the second or third decimal places but confidence intervals were roughly the same across both models and significance levels for each of the paths did not differ between the two models.

Main Question

Does this model-building approach for the improvement of fit indices seem okay from a statistical standpoint, given the large number of residual covariances added (117 in total across both level-1 and level-2) while accounting for the similarly large total number of items present at each level of the model (29 items at level-1 and 65 items at level-2)?

As can be noticed above, all fit indices other than SRMR-between look okay after the first three batches of item-level residual covariances are added to the measurement model. The remaining four batches (batch 4, 5, 6, and 7) are largely tackling the improvement of SRMR-between (from .095 in the batch 3 model to .083 in the batch 7 model).

Are there any alternatives you would suggest to keep the model more parsimonious if it offers clear advantages to the rigor of the model and helps reduce the total number of parameters in the model specified from my end?

Thanks so much for your attention. Any help is appreciated!

Tingshu

Here are my comments

####

Why should I include std.lv <http://std.lv> = T? I thought the right way is to fix the first loading to 1.0 and freely estimate others?

####
There are a couple different ways to identify the factors, as you mention the most common (default) method is marker variable (fixing a factor loading to 1), the second most common is fixed factor variance (std.lv <http://std.lv>=T). The identification method does not affect the model fit, or standardized parameters. But it affects the metric of interpretation for the unstandardized paramaters. With marker variable, the factor mean and variances are in function of the items that has the factor loading to 1. Whith fixed factor variance, the metric and interpretation of the factors is as an standardized metric (mean = 0, variance = 1). I strongly prefer fix factor variance, as the metric does not depend on a single variable, but still some people prefer marker variable.

####

I excluded estimator = “MLR” because it gave me a warning, but why? When should I use it? (I read the function description and still didn’t understand)

####
MLR adjusts the chi-square and standard errors for non-normal data distribituions (it doesnt change the parameter estimates). So, it is not a required to use it, in case you dont need to adjust for non-normality, using the default ML is fine. Now depending on what the warning is, might represent more serious problems. But is it works well with ML I dont think there is mayor concerns

####

For a brief background, I'm estimating the level and slope of well-being across 3 waves of data, where well-being was measured by a group of same 5 manifest variables at each wave. I encountered the same lv variances are negative error as Manuel, but adding std.lv <http://std.lv> = T solved it.

####
With 3 time points you are at the minimum number of time points, so be aware of possible limitations becasue of this. The latent variances were negative because they were defined in function of the choosen indicator, when you changed to std.lv <http://std.lv>=T the factor variance was in function of the standardized metric. Another possible solution for that, with marker variable is to use another variane as the one with the fixed factor loading. But again, I prefer and recommend std.lv <http://std.lv>=T

Hope this helps

> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > # * 3.1 Steinmetz, 2014 ---------------------------------------------------
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > # corrected chi-square differences test
> > > > > > > CorrDiff <- function(fit.baseline, fit.restricted) # basline = model with less degrees of freedom
> > > > > > > {
> > > > > > >   Corrc2Base <- fitMeasures(fit.baseline)[[6]] # corrected chi-square value
> > > > > > >   MLc2Base <- fitMeasures(fit.baseline)[[3]] # uncorrected chi-square value
> > > > > > >   dfBase <- fitMeasures(fit.baseline)[[4]] # degrees of freedom
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >   Corrc2Rest <- fitMeasures(fit.restricted)[[6]]
> > > > > > >   MLc2Rest <- fitMeasures(fit.restricted)[[3]]
> > > > > > >   dfRest <- fitMeasures(fit.restricted)[[4]]
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >   c0 <- MLc2Rest / Corrc2Rest
> > > > > > >   c1 <- MLc2Base / Corrc2Base
> > > > > > >   cd <- (dfRest*c0-dfBase*c1)/(dfRest-dfBase)
> > > > > > >   CorrDiff <- (MLc2Rest-MLc2Base)/cd # corrected difference test statistic T_d^*
> > > > > > >   dfDiff <- dfRest - dfBase
> > > > > > >   pDiff <- 1-pchisq(CorrDiff, dfDiff)
> > > > > > >   result <- list(Corr.chisq.difference = CorrDiff,
> > > > > > >                  df.difference=dfDiff, p.value=pDiff)
> > > > > > >   return(result)
> > > > > > > }
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > # model comparison
> > > > > > > CorrDiff(fit_configural_boredom, fit_weak_boredom)
> > > > > > > CorrDiff(fit_weak_boredom, fit_strong_boredom)
> > > > > > > CorrDiff(fit_strong_boredom, fit_strict_boredom)

messages.body_plain:
Dear lavaan users,

I'm looking for advice on our mediation model with:
- predictor X (continuous variable), the volume of a specific brain region (Heschl's gyrus)
- mediator M (continuous variable), a behavioral measure of risk for reading difficulties
- outcome Y (continuous variable), the behaviorally measured reading ability.

Since the value of predictor X is known to be very dependent on total brain volume, we would like to control for this (by including total brain volume as a covariate C). However, theoretically it does not make a lot of sense to also include the total brain volume as a covariate on M or Y. Could I use the model syntax below (only including the covariate C on X), or would that not have the desired effect (i.e. controlling for total brain volume when investigating the volume of one specific brain region)?

Y~ c*X
M ~ a*X
Y~ b*M

X ~ C

ab := a*b
total := c + (a*b)

Kind regards,
Lauren

messages.subject: Re: Meaning of ~~ in lavaan
messages.subject_clean: Meaning of ~~ in lavaan
messages.body_plain:
A quick way to check what the model will be, using only the model syntax, is to call the lavaan function (sem, cfa, etc.) without the data and then print the parameter table:

Model <- "
# regression 1
Y ~ X + W
# regression 2
X ~ Z + W

Y~~NA*X
"

library(lavaan)
#> This is lavaan 0.6-11
#> lavaan is FREE software! Please report any bugs.
parameterTable(sem(Model))
#>    id lhs op rhs user block group free ustart exo label plabel start est se
#> 1   1   Y  ~   X    1     1     1    1     NA   0         .p1.     0   0 NA
#> 2   2   Y  ~   W    1     1     1    2     NA   0         .p2.     0   0 NA
#> 3   3   X  ~   Z    1     1     1    3     NA   0         .p3.     0   0 NA
#> 4   4   X  ~   W    1     1     1    4     NA   0         .p4.     0   0 NA
#> 5   5   Y ~~   X    1     1     1    5     NA   0         .p5.     0   0 NA
#> 6   6   Y ~~   Y    0     1     1    6     NA   0         .p6.     1   1 NA
#> 7   7   X ~~   X    0     1     1    7     NA   0         .p7.     1   1 NA
#> 8   8   W ~~   W    0     1     1    0     NA   1         .p8.     1   1  0
#> 9   9   W ~~   Z    0     1     1    0     NA   1         .p9.     0   0  0
#> 10 10   Z ~~   Z    0     1     1    0     NA   1        .p10.     1   1  0
Y ~~ X is a free parameter, as shown above.

This is not a typical use of the sem and cfa functions but should usually work, except when data is needed, e.g., when the model is a multiple-group model and the number of groups is determined from the data.

lavaanify may be a better option because it is the function used to convert a model syntax to a parameter table. However, it is not easy to figure out how to set the options to make it mimic what sem or cfa does.

Regards,
Shu Fai Cheung (張樹輝)

messages.subject: Factor Scores for New Individuals
messages.subject_clean: Factor Scores for New Individuals
messages.body_plain:
I have a CFA model that I fit to a large dataset using WLSMV. I would now like to use this model to estimate factor scores for new individuals. What would be the best way to do this? I could see several options:

1) Add the new individuals to the large dataset, re-estimate the model, and save factor scores for the new individuals.

2) Save the CFA model fit object and use it with lavPredict() and newdata to estimate the factor scores for the new individuals. However, a challenge here would be if not all levels of the ordinal variables are observed in the new data.

3) Refit the CFA model to the new individuals only and estimate the factor scores from that model. However, a challenge here would be if the new data is too small.

messages.subject: Re: Meaning of ~~ in lavaan
messages.subject_clean: Meaning of ~~ in lavaan
messages.body_plain:
In general you are correct that it means that it estimates the relation of unexplained variance between variables. But it estimates the covariance, not correlation between them

On Friday, April 29, 2022 at 5:43:15 PM UTC+2 shufai...@gmail.com wrote:
> A quick way to check what the model will be, using only the model syntax, is to call the lavaan function (sem, cfa, etc.) without the data and then print the parameter table:
> Model <- "
> # regression 1
> Y ~ X + W
> # regression 2
> X ~ Z + W
>
> Y~~NA*X
> "
>
> library(lavaan)
> #> This is lavaan 0.6-11
> #> lavaan is FREE software! Please report any bugs.
> parameterTable(sem(Model))
> #>    id lhs op rhs user block group free ustart exo label plabel start est se
> #> 1   1   Y  ~   X    1     1     1    1     NA   0         .p1.     0   0 NA
> #> 2   2   Y  ~   W    1     1     1    2     NA   0         .p2.     0   0 NA
> #> 3   3   X  ~   Z    1     1     1    3     NA   0         .p3.     0   0 NA
> #> 4   4   X  ~   W    1     1     1    4     NA   0         .p4.     0   0 NA
> #> 5   5   Y ~~   X    1     1     1    5     NA   0         .p5.     0   0 NA
> #> 6   6   Y ~~   Y    0     1     1    6     NA   0         .p6.     1   1 NA
> #> 7   7   X ~~   X    0     1     1    7     NA   0         .p7.     1   1 NA
> #> 8   8   W ~~   W    0     1     1    0     NA   1         .p8.     1   1  0
> #> 9   9   W ~~   Z    0     1     1    0     NA   1         .p9.     0   0  0
> #> 10 10   Z ~~   Z    0     1     1    0     NA   1        .p10.     1   1  0
> Y ~~ X is a free parameter, as shown above.
>
> This is not a typical use of the sem and cfa functions but should usually work, except when data is needed, e.g., when the model is a multiple-group model and the number of groups is determined from the data.
>
> lavaanify may be a better option because it is the function used to convert a model syntax to a parameter table. However, it is not easy to figure out how to set the options to make it mimic what sem or cfa does.
